living.title: Living Systems
living.desc: The biological systems and structures you have learned so far.

foundations.title: Foundations of Life
foundations.desc: Foundational ideas about cells and the boundary between cellular life and viruses.

cell-theory.title: Cell Theory
cell-theory.desc: Core principles defining cells as the functional units of living systems.

notes.title: Core principles
items: Cells are the basic functional unit of life

life-boundary.title: Boundary of Life
life-boundary.desc: The distinction between cellular life and entities such as viruses.

cells.title: Cells
cells.desc: Cell boundaries, internal organization, and structural systems.

membrane.title: Plasma Membrane
membrane.desc: The phospholipid boundary separating cellular environments.

internal.title: Internal Organization
internal.desc: Internal structures and compartments of eukaryotic cells.

nucleus.title: Nucleus
nucleus.desc: Nuclear structure, genetic organization, and nucleolar function.

mitochondria.title: Mitochondria
mitochondria.desc: Structure, energetics, endosymbiosis, and apoptosis from what you have learned so far.

er.title: Endoplasmic Reticulum
er.desc: Rough and smooth ER structure and function.

golgi.title: Golgi Apparatus
golgi.desc: Modification, targeting, sorting, and packaging of cellular products.

cytoskeleton.title: Structure & Movement
cytoskeleton.desc: The cytoskeleton and structures that depend on it.

microtubules.title: Microtubules
microtubules.desc: Hollow tubulin structures involved in transport, division, and motility.

motility.title: Cilia / Flagella
motility.desc: Motility structures with a 9+2 microtubule arrangement.

prokaryotic-cell.title: Prokaryotic Cell
prokaryotic-cell.desc: Simplest organisms, including all bacteria; lack membrane-bound organelles. Genetic material is a single circular DNA molecule concentrated in the nucleoid. Understanding their structure guides antibiotic choice.

notes.title: Defining features
items: DNA concentrated in the nucleoid region (not a membrane-bound nucleus)

prokaryotic-domains.title: Prokaryotic Domains
prokaryotic-domains.desc: Two of the three domains of life contain prokaryotes: Archaea and Bacteria. Originally grouped as kingdom Monera before genetic/biochemical analysis separated them.

notes.title: Key points
items: Three domains of life: Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya
Archaea-Bacteria difference is at least as large as either vs. Eukarya
Trap: 'prokaryote' is a structural label, not an evolutionary grouping

archaea.title: Archaea
archaea.desc: Single-celled prokaryotes that look like bacteria but have eukaryote-like molecular machinery. Memory hook: molecular biology = eukaryote-like; structure & division = bacteria-like.

notes.title: Eukaryote-like (molecular biology)
items: Basis for shared-origin hypothesis with eukaryotes

notes.title: Bacteria-like (structure & division)
items: Divide by binary fission or budding

notes.title: Metabolism & habitat
items: Some photosynthetic; many chemosynthetic (energy from inorganic compounds, e.g. sulfur/nitrogen such as ammonia)
Historically extremophiles (high temp, high salinity, no light)
Now known to be widespread, including in the human body

plasmid.title: Plasmid
plasmid.desc: Small extra circular DNA, not part of the genome and not required for survival, but can confer advantages such as antibiotic resistance. Extrachromosomal circular DNA carrying beneficial genes such as antibiotic resistance and virulence factors. Episomes are the subset that can integrate into the genome.

notes.title: Key points
items: Small circular DNA separate from the chromosome
Not genomic, not required for survival
DNA in nucleoid on histone-like proteins; true histones are in Archaea

notes.title: Virulence factors & episomes
items: Virulence factors raise pathogenicity: toxin production, attachment projections, immune evasion
Episomes = plasmids capable of integrating into the genome
Episome integration of the F factor underlies Hfr

prokaryotic-ribosome.title: Prokaryotic Ribosome
prokaryotic-ribosome.desc: Prokaryotic 30S + 50S vs. eukaryotic 40S + 60S. The structural size difference enables selective antibiotic targeting (selective toxicity).

notes.title: Key points
items: Different structure enables antibiotics (tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, macrolides) to target bacteria selectively

bacteria.title: Bacteria
bacteria.desc: Prokaryotic domain; all have a cell membrane and cytoplasm. Share analogous structures with eukaryotes, so drugs achieve selectivity via biochemical differences. Host relationships range from mutualistic to pathogenic.

notes.title: Host relationships
items: Mutualistic symbiotes: both benefit (gut bacteria make vitamin K and biotin/B7)
Pathogens/parasites: no host benefit, cause disease
Extracellular example: Clostridium tetani (secretes toxins into blood)

notes.title: Classification by shape (3)
items: Spirilli = spiral (Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi, Leptospira interrogans)

bacterial-flagellum.title: Bacterial Flagellum & Chemotaxis
bacterial-flagellum.desc: Whip-like propulsion structure enabling chemotaxis (movement toward food or away from toxins). Basal body is the motor; filament is made of flagellin.

notes.title: Three parts
items: Filament: hollow, helical, made of flagellin
Basal body: the motor, anchors to membrane, rotates up to 300 Hz
Hook: transmits basal-body torque to the filament
Archaea have flagella too but structurally different

gram-staining.title: Gram Staining & Cell Envelope
gram-staining.desc: Crystal violet then safranin counterstain distinguishes wall architecture. Envelope = cell wall + cell membrane. LPS (gram-negative) drives a much stronger immune response than lipoteichoic acid (gram-positive).

notes.title: Clinical
items: Penicillin blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking to fail the wall to osmotic lysis (esp. gram-positive)
Most bacteria resistant; a few still sensitive (S. pyogenes, T. pallidum)
LPS triggers stronger inflammation than lipoteichoic acid

bacterial-metabolism.title: Aerobes & Anaerobes
bacterial-metabolism.desc: Four-way oxygen classification. High-yield trap is facultative (uses O2 when present) vs. aerotolerant (never uses O2 but is unharmed by it).

notes.title: Four categories
items: Obligate anaerobes: O2 is lethal (reactive oxygen radicals)
Facultative anaerobes: use O2 if present, switch to anaerobic if absent
Aerotolerant anaerobes: never use O2 but are not harmed by it

bacterial-growth-curve.title: Bacterial Growth Curve
bacterial-growth-curve.desc: Colony growth over time (log of number vs. time) proceeds through four ordered phases: lag, exponential/log, stationary, death.

genetic-recombination.title: Genetic Recombination
genetic-recombination.desc: Prokaryotes acquire foreign genetic material to increase diversity and drive evolution. Three mechanisms sorted by what they require: transformation (naked DNA), conjugation (contact bridge), transduction (viral vector).

binary-fission.title: Binary Fission
binary-fission.desc: Asexual reproduction in prokaryotes. Circular chromosome attaches to the cell wall and replicates while the cell grows, then the membrane and wall invaginate at the midline to yield two identical daughter cells. Faster than mitosis (no spindle).

notes.title: Steps
steps: circular chromosome attaches to cell wall
membrane and wall invaginate at midline

notes.title: Key points
items: Fewer events than mitosis, so it is fast
Ideal E. coli divides about every 20 minutes

transposon.title: Transposon
transposon.desc: Genetic elements that insert into and excise themselves from the genome. Not limited to prokaryotes (also in eukaryotes). Insertion into a coding region can disrupt that gene.

transduction.title: Transduction
transduction.desc: The only recombination process requiring a vector. A bacteriophage accidentally packages host DNA during assembly and injects it into another bacterium, where it integrates. Viruses are obligate intracellular pathogens.

conjugation.title: Conjugation & Hfr
conjugation.desc: Bacterial mating: a conjugation bridge transfers DNA unidirectionally from donor male (F+) to recipient female (F-). The bridge is built from sex pili requiring sex-factor plasmids such as the F (fertility) factor.

notes.title: F+ vs Hfr
items: Transfer is unidirectional: F+ donor to F- recipient
Bridge = sex pili on the donor; require sex-factor plasmids (F factor in E. coli)
F+ x F-: F factor is a free plasmid, copies and transfers cleanly, recipient becomes F+
Hfr (high frequency of recombination): F factor integrated into chromosome, so the cell tries to transfer the whole genome
Hfr x F-: bridge usually breaks before the full sequence (and full F factor) transfers, so recipient gains chromosomal genes but usually stays F-

transformation.title: Transformation
transformation.desc: Integration of foreign genetic material taken up from the environment, usually spilled by other bacteria that lysed. Requires no cell contact and no vector. Common in gram-negative rods.
